title: Saul Anointed, Changed, and Chosen
summary: Samuel privately anoints Saul as ruler over the LORD's inheritance and gives him three signs to confirm it. All three happen that day, and at Gibeah the Spirit of God rushes upon Saul and he prophesies with a band of prophets, to the astonishment of those who know him. Samuel then gathers Israel at Mizpah, rebukes them for rejecting God, and has the tribes present themselves before the LORD; the lot falls on Saul, who is found hiding among the baggage. The people shout for their king, though some worthless men despise him.
story: Chapter 9 ended with Samuel taking Saul aside at the edge of town to reveal God's word. Chapter 10 moves from the private anointing to the public choosing, and it shows both God's gift and Israel's ambivalence. Samuel anoints Saul and God changes his heart, yet Samuel also tells the gathered people again that in asking for a king they have rejected their God. Saul himself hides from the crowd. The chapter also plants a detail that will matter later: Samuel's command to wait seven days for him at Gilgal (verse 8), which Saul will fail to keep in chapter 13. The next chapter will give Saul the chance to prove himself.
historical:
The places named trace Saul's route home through the territory of Benjamin and its border. Rachel's tomb is placed here at Zelzah on the border of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, while Genesis 35:19 connects Rachel's burial with the road to Ephrath, which later tradition identified with Bethlehem to the south. Scholars have explained the difference by suggesting that Ephrath originally named a region near the Benjamin border, or that there were different traditions about the site. The Oak of Tabor and Zelzah cannot be located with certainty. Gibeah of God, where the Philistines had an outpost, may be the same as Saul's hometown Gibeah or the nearby town of Geba; the similar names make identification difficult.

The mention of a Philistine outpost in the heart of Benjamin shows how far Philistine control had reached into the hill country, and it explains why the people wanted a military leader. Mizpah, where Samuel gathers the people, was the same place where Israel had repented and won a victory in chapter 7.
cultural:
Anointing with oil was a sign of consecration used for priests and kings across the ancient Near East; in Israel it signified that God had chosen and set the person apart. Samuel's kiss likely expressed respect or homage. The three signs Samuel gives were a common way of confirming a prophetic word: when the predicted events happen, the recipient can trust the larger promise.

The group of prophets Saul meets represents a kind of prophetic community that appears at several points in the Old Testament, sometimes called the sons of the prophets. Their prophesying accompanied by music seems to have been an ecstatic, visible experience, quite different from the spoken oracles of later prophets like Isaiah; music is associated with prophecy elsewhere too (2 Kings 3:15). Choosing by lot was a way of seeking God's decision, and Israel used it for serious matters such as dividing the land and identifying a guilty person (Joshua 7). The people's shout, Long live the king, was the traditional acclamation. Samuel's writing of the rights of kingship on a scroll and laying it before the LORD reflects the principle of Deuteronomy 17:18-20, that the king must live under a written law.
literary: The chapter has two main scenes: the private confirmation of Saul's anointing (verses 1-16) and the public selection at Mizpah (verses 17-27). The first is full of fulfilled predictions; the narrator's brief statement that all these signs came to pass that day shows that God stands behind Samuel's word. The famous question “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (verses 11-12) became a proverb, and a second version of its origin appears in 19:24, where it takes on a darker meaning. Its tone here is ambiguous: surprise, perhaps mockery, at seeing the ordinary son of Kish among prophets. The reply “And who is their father?” is also unclear; it may mean that prophetic gifts don't come by inheritance, so anyone can receive them. The public scene has a touch of comedy: the lot falls on Saul, but he can't be found, and God has to reveal that he is hiding among the baggage. The chapter ends with a contrast between the valiant men whose hearts God touched and the worthless men who despise Saul.

outline.t: Three signs and the command to wait at Gilgal
Saul's heart changed; the Spirit comes and he prophesies
Saul keeps silent about the kingship
Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah and rebukes them
Saul chosen by lot and found hiding
The rights of kingship written; supporters and despisers

doctrines.note: The Spirit of God rushes upon Saul, empowering him for his task and bringing him to prophesy. In the Old Testament the Spirit frequently comes upon leaders to equip them for particular roles, as with the judges. Saul's later loss of the Spirit (16:14) shows that in this setting the Spirit's empowering for office could be withdrawn.

The lot, the fulfilled signs, and the anointing all show that God chose Saul. The people wanted a king, but God determined who it would be, and the chapter repeatedly makes clear that the king is the LORD's choice.

Samuel calls Israel the LORD's inheritance and writes down the rights of kingship before the LORD. The king is not an absolute ruler but a steward over a people that belongs to God, bound by a written charter. Israel's kingship is meant to be kingship under God's law.

words.note: Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. When used of God, it refers to his active presence and power. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Saul as it had come upon judges like Gideon and Samson, equipping him for leadership. The same word describes the Spirit that will later depart from Saul.

Tsalach, to rush upon, to come mightily. The verb is used of the Spirit coming on Samson (Judges 14:6) and later on David (16:13). It suggests a sudden, powerful, even overwhelming experience rather than a gradual influence.

Naba, to prophesy. In this chapter the verb describes an ecstatic, visible experience shared by a group, often accompanied by music. It later came to refer mostly to delivering God's message in words. Saul's prophesying marks him publicly as someone God's Spirit has touched.

Haphakh, to turn or overturn. Samuel tells Saul he will be turned into a different person (verse 6), and the narrator says God changed his heart (verse 9), using the same verb. It describes a genuine, God-given change, though the story will show that Saul's later choices matter as well.

christ: Anointing and the coming of the Spirit are joined in this chapter, as they are in the ministry of Jesus. At his baptism the Spirit descends on Jesus, and in the synagogue at Nazareth he reads from Isaiah 61, announcing that the Spirit of the Lord is upon him because he has anointed him (Luke 4:18). The title Christ means anointed one. Saul receives the Spirit for a task and later loses it; the Gospels present Jesus as the one on whom the Spirit remains (John 1:32-33) and who pours out the Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33). This is a pattern of anointing and empowerment that runs from Israel's kings to Jesus, not a prediction contained in 1 Samuel 10 itself.

hard.q: If God changed Saul's heart and gave him the Spirit, how could Saul fail so badly later?
hard.a: Saul's story is one of the Bible's sharpest puzzles about divine gifts and human responsibility. Some readers argue that the change of heart and the coming of the Spirit here equipped Saul for kingship, giving him courage and ability, without implying the kind of lasting inner renewal the New Testament describes; the Spirit in the Old Testament often empowered people for service, and could leave (16:14). Others think Saul did experience a genuine turning toward God, but that God's gifts do not remove human responsibility, and Saul's later disobedience was a real turning away. Still others focus on the text's own details, noting that even here Saul's response is uncertain: he hides from his uncle what Samuel said, and hides among the baggage when chosen, which some read as humility and others as fear. The chapter does not settle the question, but the rest of Saul's story shows that receiving a gift from God is no guarantee of using it faithfully.

questions: Saul received signs, a changed heart, and the Spirit. What gifts or confirmations has God given you, and how are you responding to them?
Saul hid among the baggage when he was chosen. Is it humility or fear that keeps people from stepping into what God has called them to do?
Samuel wrote down the rights of kingship and laid them before the LORD. Why do leaders, even good ones, need to be bound by something outside their own will?
